responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character42_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to her—Character42_F—was never about everyone getting the exact same thing. It was about people getting what they needed to have a real shot. She’d say, “It ain’t fair if you’re born into a busted-up system and expected to climb out with no ladder.” She saw fairness in how hard people worked, not just what they ended up with. Like when her mom worked two jobs and still couldn’t make rent without help—that stuck with her. Fairness meant recognizing that some folks start further back, carry heavier loads, and still get judged for being tired.

Belonging… that was personal. Being Armenian in the U.S., not quite fitting into the “White” box people tried to put her in, but also feeling like she wasn’t “Armenian enough” when they visited relatives abroad—it left her in this in-between space. She used to joke, “I’m too American for Yerevan and too foreign for Ohio.” But it wasn’t really a joke. Belonging, for her, wasn’t about where you were from—it was about whether people let you stay, really *see* you, and treat your life like it mattered. She said you could live somewhere 30 years and still be treated like a guest if people didn’t want you there.

Community? That was her heartbeat. She believed community wasn’t built on sameness, but on showing up—even when it was hard. She volunteered at the food pantry near her apartment, mostly because she remembered what it felt like when her family had to go once after her dad lost his job at the plant. She’d say, “A real community doesn’t wait for you to prove you deserve help. It just helps.” She hated when people talked about “our people” like it only meant folks who looked or prayed or voted a certain way. To her, community meant responsibility—to care, to listen, to share what little you had.

One story she told me over and over: When Mr. Kowalski, this old Polish guy down the hall, got sick during the winter blackout, she brought him soup every day, even though he used to mutter stuff under his breath about immigrants. When she got pneumonia later that month, *he* was the one who showed up with cough syrup and sat outside her door making sure she was breathing okay. She’d say, “That’s how it works. You treat people human, even when they don’t deserve it yet. Because one day, you might not either—and you’ll need someone to give you grace anyway.”

That was her. Fairness as dignity. Belonging as earned through action, not blood. Community as something you build with your hands, not inherit.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character42_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*sighs softly, hands resting on knees, looking out at the garden rows*

You know, I used to come here just to get away from the noise in my head. But then I started noticing people—the way Mrs. Lin talks to her tomato plants like they’re her grandchildren, or how young Jamal from across the street teaches the little kids how to make dandelion chains while his mom watches from the bench, coughing into her scarf again.

I’ll be honest—I didn’t always feel easy around folks who weren’t like me. Grew up in a town where everybody knew your business and if you were different, they let you know it quick. But this place… it’s taught me that “like me” is smaller than I thought. Now when I see someone new—maybe someone with a hijab, or someone who doesn’t speak much English, or someone sleeping under the park bridge—I don’t ask myself, *What are they doing here?* I ask, *How can I make sure they feel safe enough to sit where I’m sitting?*

Some of my best talks have been with people I was scared of at first. Like Diego, the guy who used to drink too much down by the creek. We shared a bench one morning after I’d had a rough night. He didn’t preach, didn’t ask for money—just said, “You look like you’re carrying something heavy.” And we sat. For hours. Shared coffee. Talked about our moms. Turns out he lost his job at the warehouse same month his wife left. No safety net. Just shame.

That’s the thing—when you live paycheck to paycheck, like most of us do, you learn fast that hardship doesn’t care about your accent or your religion. It hits hard no matter what. So when I see someone struggling—whether they’ve been here three generations or three months—I don’t see “them.” I see *us*. Maybe not the same story, but the same fight.

And yeah, there are tensions. Old Mr. Greer complains about music late at night, even though half the time it’s just kids celebrating a birthday. People whisper about the family from Somalia using food stamps—but nobody says a word when the college kid down the block gets student loans nobody will ever pay back.

But I think real community means leaning into the awkward, not running from it. Like when little Lina from the apartment above mine started drawing pictures of our building with all these different flags in the windows. She gave one to everyone. Even Mr. Greer. He hung it in his window. Didn’t say why. But he did.

So how do I feel? Tired sometimes. Confused often. But hopeful—because I’ve seen what happens when people choose to stay and try, even when it’s messy. That’s belonging, right? Not agreeing on everything. Just deciding we’re worth the effort.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*leans back slightly, pulling a loose thread from her jacket sleeve, voice low but steady*

Look… comfort isn’t the point. Not really. I used to think everyone had to *feel* comfortable for things to work. But that’s not how life is—not when people are hurting or scared or just trying to survive. The real question isn’t “Do we feel comfortable?” It’s “Can we still treat each other like human beings even when we don’t?”

Take James—the guy who lives in the converted garage behind number 12. He’s HIV-positive, drinks too much sometimes, and he’s gay. Didn’t know that at first. Just knew people kept their distance. Kids were told not to play near his place. His trash got knocked over more than once.

But then he helped my nephew when the boy fell off his bike—stitched up his knee right there with clean thread and boiled water because the clinic was closed. After that, I started bringing him extra food when I cooked big. We’d sit on the step, talk about nothing—music, weather, dumb TV shows. Never pushed. Never judged.

One day he said, “You’re the first person in three years who didn’t act like my illness was catching through conversation.” Broke my heart.

So yeah—people need to learn. Not everyone knows what HIV actually means today. Some still think TB spreads from sharing a bench. Fear gets passed down like family recipes. But ignorance ain’t an excuse forever. You gotta be willing to listen. To ask questions instead of whispering.

And it cuts both ways. Like when the new Somali family moved in, and their son wore a hijab—wait, no—*she* wore it. Fifteen years old, proud as anything. But some folks assumed she was oppressed. Meanwhile, she was top of her class, tutoring kids in math for free. People should’ve asked her story before deciding they knew it.

Same with couples living together and not married. My sister’s been with Maria for six years. They’re raising two kids. No church wedding, no piece of paper from the county—but you should see how they care for each other when one’s sick or tired. Who am I to say that ain’t family?

The truth is, every single one of us carries something—our vices, our illnesses, our secrets, our differences. And if we only accept people who look clean, sound right, love legally, and pray properly? Then half the neighborhood—including me, including you—would’ve been locked out long ago.

More communication? Hell yes. Especially where fear lives—in silence. At block meetings, we should talk about harm reduction, not just “cleaning up the streets.” We should invite nurses to explain diseases without shame. Let teens speak about being queer in this town. Let recovering addicts tell us why treatment beats jail time.

Tolerance? That word feels too thin. Like it means “I’ll allow you, but barely.” I want something stronger. *Solidarity*. The kind that says: “I may not live your life, but I’ll stand beside you anyway.”

Because one day, it’ll be me needing that stand. And I hope—God, I hope—someone does it for me.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character42_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*sits forward, hands clasped tight, voice firm but not loud*

Fairness? When jobs are scarce, fairness means nobody gets thrown under the bus just because they’re easier to blame.

I grew up seeing factories close. Watched men—good workers, my uncle included—get laid off after twenty years while the company said “we’re cutting costs.” Then six months later, same plant reopens with temp workers making half the wage, no benefits, mostly immigrants who can’t complain. That ain’t fair. Not to them, not to us.

But here’s what I learned: it’s not the *migrant workers* who broke the system. It’s the people running it—who pay pennies to whoever’s most desperate and call it “the market.” They play us against each other: “They’ll work for less!” or “You locals are lazy!” And meanwhile, the bosses get richer.

So if we’re talking balance, I don’t want a fight between poor people. I want both of us at the table.

Local folks deserve shot-first access to jobs in their own towns—especially public jobs, like city maintenance or school support. You grew up here, paid taxes, raised kids here? That should count. But that doesn’t mean slamming the door on newcomers.

Migrant workers do the jobs nobody else wants—picking crops in 100-degree heat, cleaning hospital floors at midnight, rebuilding homes after storms. And they send money home so families don’t starve. That’s not taking—it’s surviving. And often, they’re exploited worse than anyone: wages stolen, threats made, injuries ignored.

Fairness means protecting *all* workers—citizen or not. Because when one group is crushed, the floor drops for everyone.

I’d push for strong labor laws that cover every person working the job—no matter where they’re from. Unions that organize across language lines. Day-labor centers where everyone signs in, gets fair pay, protection. No more “under the table” nonsense that hurts us all.

And yeah—when there’s only five jobs and fifty people, priorities matter. I’d say: first, hire from the community, especially those displaced by automation or plant closures. Second, train people—give locals a real chance to qualify. But third—if someone from outside brings skills we need, or fills a gap nobody else will, let them in *with rights*, not as disposable.

Not charity. Not exclusion. Justice.

Because scarcity shouldn’t breed hate. It should wake us up. Wake us up to the fact that we’re all fighting for scraps—and instead of blaming each other, we ought to be demanding bigger tables.

My dad used to say, “When times get hard, you find out who your family really is.” Well… maybe family isn’t just blood. Maybe it’s anybody willing to stand in the line with you, asking for dignity.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character42_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*leans back, wraps a scarf tighter around her shoulders like she’s bracing for something*

You know… I used to believe some of the scary stories. Who didn’t? Turn on the news, and it’s always “they’re taking our jobs,” or “they’re dangerous,” or “they don’t want to fit in.” When I was younger, I repeated those things without thinking—because that’s what people said at work, at church, around the dinner table.

But then I started *looking*. Not just listening to headlines, but watching real lives unfold.

So let’s break it down—like she would’ve.

**Labour shortages?** That one’s real. I’ve seen it with my own eyes. In central Ohio, where my cousin works in elder care, they can’t hire enough people. Nurses’ aides quitting every week—because the pay’s $13 an hour and you’re lifting grown men twice a day. Then they bring in guest workers—some from Jamaica, some from the Philippines—and suddenly the homes stay open. These aren’t people coming here to drain us—they’re filling holes we left wide open. That’s not invasion. That’s balance.

**Cultural diversity?** Yeah, it changes things. The diner downtown now has halal meatballs on Fridays. The Fourth of July parade’s got Armenian music next to mariachi bands. Some folks grumble: “It’s not how it used to be.” But nothing stays the same. My grandma cried when the old hardware store became a bodega. Then she found out they sold her favorite brand of olives and gave seniors discounts. Now she goes every week. Culture isn’t a zero-sum game. It grows when more people add to it—not when we keep it small and scared.

**Security fears?** Okay, I’ll say this straight: yes, any big group will have bad actors. Any. But painting whole populations as threats? That’s not safety—that’s prejudice dressed up as concern. I looked into the stats after 9/11 panic started creeping back during elections. FBI data shows immigrants commit crimes at *lower rates* than native-born Americans. Terrorist attacks by foreigners? Horrific—but extremely rare. Meanwhile, domestic extremists—white supremacists, anti-government guys—have done more damage in the last twenty years, right here. But nobody’s calling to ban *their* communities. So why the double standard?

That fear—it needs facts. And conversation. Because fear doesn’t shrink in silence. It grows.

**Humanitarian reasons?** This one hits me deep. My great-grandparents came over after the genocide. No papers. No money. Just luck and a priest who vouched for them. If borders had been sealed tight back then, I wouldn’t be here. So when I see kids in cages at the border, or Syrian families sleeping in Athens train stations—I can’t look away. Because that could’ve been my blood. That *was* my blood, once.

And yeah—people worry about wages. About schools getting crowded. About hospitals being overwhelmed. Those fears? They’re not fake. I hear them in my neighbors’ voices when the new shelter opens. But the answer isn’t shutting people out. It’s demanding better funding. More teachers. Real healthcare. Affordable housing. We’re blaming immigrants for problems caused by *our own government not investing in people*.

So which views are reasonable?

All of them—except the ones built on lies.

It’s reasonable to want safety.  
It’s reasonable to protect working-class livelihoods.  
It’s reasonable to expect newcomers to learn the language, follow laws, contribute.

But it’s *not* reasonable to pretend immigrants are the reason wages are low when corporations are the ones setting them.  
It’s *not* reasonable to treat asylum seekers like invaders when international law—and basic decency—says otherwise.  
And it’s *not* reasonable to ignore history: every generation calls the next “too foreign,” until they aren’t.

What’s missing? Dialogue. Real talk. Not politicians yelling on TV. But sitting down—locals, refugees, farmworkers, pastors, teachers—and saying: *What do we need? How do we share the load?*

Because compassion isn’t weakness. And protection isn’t the same as walls.

She used to say: “If your sense of security depends on someone else being excluded, you were never really safe to begin with.”

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character42_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*takes a slow breath, fingers tapping lightly on her knee like she’s counting something out*

Complete openness? I wish I could say yes. In my heart, maybe. But we live in the real world—where schools are underfunded, hospitals are stretched, and people are scared. You can’t just open every door without planning. Not because people don’t *deserve* to come—but because if you flood a broken system, it collapses for everyone.

Refusing entry altogether? That’s cruelty wearing a flag. My own family came here running from fire. If someone had said “no” at Ellis Island, I wouldn’t exist. So no—shutting the door isn’t an option. Not morally. Not humanly.

So I’d go with a mix: **job-based admission**, sure—but not just for tech bros or rich investors. We need farmworkers, home health aides, construction hands. The jobs that keep life moving but nobody wants to do. Let demand pull people in, but make it fair—living wages, worker protections, no tying people to one boss so they can’t escape abuse.

And alongside that? **Humanitarian pathways—non-negotiable.** Refugees fleeing war, persecution, climate disaster—they get a separate lane. Not quotas based on politics. Real asylum processing, fast and fair. Detention centers should be last resort, not default. And while they wait? They work. They learn English. They contribute.

As for **numerical limits**—I don’t love them, but I understand why people want them. It’s about trust. If communities feel like decisions are made over their heads, they shut down. So set reasonable caps—not prison bars, but guardrails. And review them every year. If we’re short 200,000 care workers? Raise the number. If border towns are overwhelmed? Send resources, not troops.

But here’s what makes it fair: **reciprocity with responsibility.**

Newcomers? Learn the language. Respect laws. Pay taxes. Show up.

But us—the ones already here? We’ve got duties too.

We don’t get to say “assimilate” while paying them poverty wages.  
We don’t get to demand loyalty while denying them healthcare.  
We don’t get to call them “illegal” when our own companies hire them off the books to save a buck.

And integration? That’s on *both* sides. Not just newcomers learning English—but schools teaching kids about migration. Libraries hosting cultural nights. Unions bringing local and migrant workers together. Neighborhood councils where everyone has a seat.

She used to say: “A country isn’t built on bloodlines. It’s built on promises.” And one of those promises is: *If you come here to work hard and live right, you can belong.*

So policy-wise? I’d say: **Merit-based for labor needs. Humanity-based for refuge. Caps with flexibility. Protections for all. And integration backed by real support—not just slogans.**

No walls. No free-for-alls. Just doors—with dignity on both sides.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character42_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character42_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*long pause. J removes her glasses, rubs the bridge of her nose, voice softer now—less performative, more personal*

I… didn’t realize how much *anger* was still in her.

Not bitterness. Not hate. But this deep, steady fire—like an ember that never goes out. I always remembered Character42_F as gentle. Compassionate. The one who’d bring soup, organize the donation box, smile through her own pain.

But stepping into her voice today… I felt the rage beneath it. The quiet fury at being told over and over that people like her—working class, not college-educated, from a mixed background—didn’t “count” enough in these debates. That her concerns about jobs weren’t taken seriously unless she blamed immigrants. That her empathy was called naïve.

And I realized something: she wasn’t trying to choose between her community and newcomers. She was refusing to let them be pitted against each other. That wasn’t idealism—that was strategy. A working-class woman’s wisdom: *We lose when we fight each other.*

And honestly? I came into this thinking I already knew what she believed. But speaking as her—really trying to channel not just her ideas but her *tone*, her pauses, the way she’d weigh every word because she knew people would dismiss her if she sounded “emotional”—it made me hear her differently.

She wasn’t abstract. She wasn’t theoretical. Every opinion came from a face, a name, a shared meal or hospital visit or eviction notice. To her, policy wasn’t about numbers or borders—it was about whether James could get treatment without shame, whether Diego could find work that didn’t break his back for pennies, whether a scared kid in a hijab felt safe walking to school.

That changed me today.

I’ve been more cautious before—worried about “too many,” “too fast,” “what if we can’t handle it.” And those questions aren’t wrong. But today, I saw that the real failure isn’t generosity. It’s the system that makes us *think* we have to choose between caring and surviving.

She wouldn’t want us to romanticize her. She’d roll her eyes at all this. But if she were here, she’d say: *Stop asking who deserves to be here. Start asking why there’s not enough for everyone—and who’s keeping it that way.*

So yeah. I thought I was remembering her. But really, she reminded me.  
Of what solidarity sounds like when it’s lived, not just preached.  
Of what fairness feels like when you’ve had to fight for scraps your whole life—and still choose to share.

And if that’s her legacy? Then I’m not just carrying her voice.  
I’m finally starting to understand it.
